vignette:
The Weight of Numbers

Maya is twenty-two years old, the eldest daughter of a close-knit Colombian family who immigrated to the United States when she was a child. She works as a junior accountant at a mid-sized firm downtown, a job she chose deliberately - numbers, she says, are reliable. They follow rules. They don't surprise you.

Three years ago, when Maya was nineteen and her little brother Tomás was six, he collapsed at the kitchen table while doing his homework. What followed was six weeks in a pediatric ICU, a diagnosis of bacterial meningitis, two surgeries, and a period during which the doctors told her parents, gently but plainly, that Tomás might not survive. Maya's parents spoke limited English, and so it fell to her - the bilingual eldest, the responsible one - to translate the medical updates, the consent forms, the conversations about what "comfort care" might mean. She sat in waiting rooms under fluorescent lights, turning terrifying sentences from English into Spanish, watching her mother's face change as the words landed.

Tomás survived. He came home with some hearing loss in his left ear and a scar along his side, and within a year he was back to being a loud, energetic child who left his shoes in the middle of the hallway. Her parents speak of it now as a miracle, something to be grateful for. Maya agrees with them, out loud, when the subject comes up.

But something in her did not return to normal the way Tomás did.

She finds herself checking on him constantly - texting her mother three or four times a day to ask if he seems okay, driving to her parents' house on weeknights for no clear reason, standing in the doorway of his room and watching him sleep. If he doesn't respond to a text quickly, her mind moves immediately to the worst possible image: his small body in that hospital bed, the ventilator, the sound of the monitors. The image doesn't fade on its own. It takes her a long time to pull herself back.

At work, Maya is precise and capable, and her supervisors have noticed. She is the first one in and often the last to leave. She has built her professional life around the comfort of systems and order, and she is good at it. But there are afternoons when a coworker mentions a sick child, or when she overhears someone in the break room talking about a hospital visit, and she has to excuse herself to the bathroom and sit in the stall until her breathing slows. She has learned to do this quietly enough that no one has asked.

She sleeps poorly. She wakes at two or three in the morning with her heart going fast, sometimes from a dream she can't fully remember - hospital hallways, the particular smell of antiseptic, her own voice saying words in Spanish that she doesn't want to say. She lies in the dark and runs through spreadsheets in her mind, sometimes literally, trying to replace the images with something neutral and structured.

She hasn't told anyone about this. Her parents are so relieved, so focused on Tomás's continued recovery, that she doesn't want to introduce a new worry. Her friends know she went through "a hard time" with her brother's illness, but she has always moved the conversation along before it could go deeper. She presents as composed, a little reserved, someone who has her life organized and under control.

What Maya carries privately is the memory of being nineteen and alone in a hospital corridor, holding a clipboard, translating the sentence we need to prepare you for the possibility that he won't make it into the language her mother would understand. She did it. She held herself together. And in some part of her, she is still standing in that hallway, still holding the clipboard, still waiting to find out whether her brother is going to live.
